interest: Traces U.S. thinking on the Emperor from 1941 to 1944, including Cabot Coville's 1943 case for keeping the throne.
overview: This file (State Department decimal file 894.001, October 1941 – November 1944) focuses on United States and Allied policy regarding the Japanese Emperor and the imperial institution across three distinct wartime and prewar moments. The collection opens with an extensive March 1943 research study by Cabot Coville of the Division of Political Studies analyzing the historical development, constitutional powers, psychological hold, and postwar alternatives concerning the Japanese emperorship, concluding that retaining a reformed, non-militaristic monarchy would best preserve social order and facilitate democratic reforms in postwar Japan. The file also includes a July 1944 telegram from Ambassador W. Averell Harriman in Moscow reporting Soviet press coverage of the newly formed Koiso-Yonai Cabinet in Tokyo, followed by November 1944 correspondence between the British Political Warfare Mission, the State Department, and the Office of War Information (OWI) debating psychological warfare directives and advising against Allied propaganda attacks on Emperor Hirohito or the imperial institution. Finally, the file contains October 1941 internal State Department deliberations—notably featuring vigorous opposition from Political Adviser Stanley K. Hornbeck on appeasement grounds—regarding a proposed presidential congratulatory telegram from Franklin D. Roosevelt to the Emperor on the marriage of his brother, Prince Mikasa.

subfiles.about: A comprehensive State Department research paper analyzing the historical origins, constitutional authority, political manipulation, psychological influence, and postwar disposition of the Japanese imperial institution.
subfiles.from: Cabot Coville, Division of Political Studies, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Prepared by Cabot Coville for the Division of Political Studies, this extensive study examines whether the institution of the Japanese emperorship should be tolerated after the defeat of Japan. Coville traces the historical evolution of the throne, noting that the modern all-powerful emperorship was deliberately created by Meiji statesmen rather than being an immutable ancient fixture, and explains how the military exploited the practice of direct access to dominate state policy. He evaluates three postwar alternatives: maintaining the status quo, abolishing the monarchy, or preserving a reformed emperorship stripped of militarist influence. Coville concludes that preserving a modified emperorship offers the best prospect for domestic order and successful reform in postwar Japan.
subfiles.title: Report by Cabot Coville on the Status of the Japanese Emperor

subfiles.about: An incoming diplomatic telegram from Moscow reporting Soviet press coverage of Domei despatches on the formation and imperial presentation of the new Koiso Cabinet.
subfiles.from: W. Averell Harriman, U.S. Ambassador to the Soviet Union (Moscow)
subfiles.summary: Harriman relays Soviet press reports on the Koiso Cabinet, formed July 22, 1944, with Yonai, Sugiyama and Shigemitsu.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Ambassador Harriman (Moscow) Reporting Formation of the Koiso Cabinet

subfiles.about: A letter forwarding British comments on a draft Office of War Information directive concerning Allied propaganda policy toward the Japanese Emperor.
subfiles.from: F. G. Healey, British Political Warfare Mission, Washington
subfiles.summary: F. G. Healey of the British Political Warfare Mission sends Lockhart his comments on OWI guidance about the Emperor and asks for State Department views.
subfiles.title: Letter from F. G. Healey to Frank P. Lockhart regarding OWI Guidance on the Japanese Emperor
subfiles.to: Frank P. Lockhart, Department of State, Washington

subfiles.about: A letter expressing State Department concurrence with British views on propaganda guidance regarding the Japanese Emperor, accompanied by a retained duplicate file copy.
subfiles.from: Frank P. Lockhart, Department of State, Washington
subfiles.summary: Lockhart tells Healey that Dooman and Dickover largely agree with British comments on OWI guidance about the Emperor.
subfiles.title: Letter from Frank P. Lockhart to F. G. Healey Concurring with British Guidance on the Emperor
subfiles.to: F. G. Healey, British Political Warfare Mission, Washington

subfiles.about: An enclosed British memorandum-letter offering detailed observations on an OWI draft directive regarding the Japanese Emperor and psychological warfare strategy.
subfiles.from: F. G. Healey, British Political Warfare Mission, Washington
subfiles.summary: Healey, with Sir George Sansom, urges OWI to target militarists, not the Emperor or the imperial institution, and not to call it 'outmoded.'
subfiles.title: Letter from F. G. Healey to George Taylor on OWI Directives Concerning the Japanese Emperor
subfiles.to: George E. Taylor, Office of War Information, Washington

subfiles.about: An internal protocol memorandum questioning whether the Division of Protocol should initial a proposed presidential congratulatory message to the Japanese Emperor.
subfiles.from: Stanley Woodward, Division of Protocol, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Stanley Woodward advises Summerlin that Protocol should not initial a congratulatory telegram to the Emperor without instructions from Hull or Welles.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Stanley Woodward to George T. Summerlin regarding Congratulatory Message Protocol
subfiles.to: George T. Summerlin, Chief, Division of Protocol, Department of State

subfiles.about: A memorandum by Political Adviser Stanley K. Hornbeck strongly objecting to sending a presidential congratulatory telegram to the Japanese Emperor on appeasement grounds.
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Adviser on Political Relations, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck calls a presidential wedding telegram to Hirohito 'just plain silly,' warning it would look like appeasement.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Stanley K. Hornbeck Opposing Congratulatory Telegram to the Japanese Emperor

subfiles.about: A memorandum from the Division of Far Eastern Affairs submitting a draft congratulatory telegram from President Roosevelt to Emperor Hirohito for Under Secretary Welles's decision.
subfiles.from: Robert Lacy Smyth, Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Robert Lacy Smyth tells Welles that Far Eastern Affairs favors a congratulatory wedding telegram to the Emperor, though Smyth himself is dubious.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Robert Lacy Smyth to Sumner Welles on Proposed Imperial Wedding Telegram
subfiles.to: Sumner Welles, Under Secretary of State

subfiles.about: A congratulatory telegram from President Franklin D. Roosevelt to Emperor Hirohito felicitating him on the marriage of his brother, Prince Mikasa.
subfiles.from: Franklin D. Roosevelt, President of the United States
subfiles.summary: Roosevelt's October 21, 1941 telegram congratulating the Emperor on Prince Mikasa's marriage to Yuriko Takagi.
subfiles.title: Telegram from President Franklin D. Roosevelt to the Emperor of Japan
